account: The 100,000 Genomes Project rare-disease diagnosis pilot returned results to the Genomic Medicine Centers of the English National Health Service from May 2016 through April 2019. It applied Exomiser's phenotype-based prioritization to genomes from 2,183 families. The pilot report appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine on 11 November 2021. Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders. The virtual panel-based pipeline alone made 322 (66%) of the 490 diagnoses that were based on single-nucleotide variants or indels. With Exomiser's ranking, diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates. Of the 490 diagnoses, 92% came from applied gene panels or Exomiser's top five candidates. Clinicians reported that 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses, 25%, were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes, surveillance recommendations, clinical trial eligibility and reproductive planning. The authors report that a diagnosis of CTPS1 deficiency in a 10-year-old girl, admitted to intensive care with life-threatening chicken pox after a seven-year diagnostic odyssey, enabled a curative bone marrow transplantation. They report that a diagnosis of transcobalamin II deficiency, made after a male neonate died at four months with no diagnosis, let his younger brother start weekly hydroxocobalamin injections that prevent metabolic decompensation. The authors do not say whether Exomiser or the applied panels found either variant. In December 2024 Exomiser's developers and a Genomics England scientist reported that a fresh run across the full project found diagnoses for 463 of 24,015 unsolved patients. In January 2025 the Hong Kong Genome Project reported that Exomiser accounted for 107 of 132 diagnoses from single-nucleotide variants and indels in 520 families and ranked 67% of them first. In October 2025 an independent group at the University of Utah and Stanford reported an optimized variant prioritization process for Exomiser and Genomiser, drawn from 386 diagnosed probands of the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. With that process, the percentage of coding diagnostic variants ranked within the top 10 candidates increased from 49.7% to 85.5%.

ai_role.statement: Exomiser scored and ranked candidate variants against each proband's phenotype. The pilot reports that diagnoses were detected in 77% of top-ranked candidate variants and that panels and Exomiser's top five were complementary. Clinical confirmation and reporting were performed by NHS diagnostic laboratories and clinicians, not by the software. Neither cited source says who developed Exomiser. The pilot's prioritization analysis was led by Damian Smedley's team at Queen Mary University of London and Genomics England, who are among the paper's authors. An independent evaluation is cited alongside it.

fields.account: The 100,000 Genomes Project rare-disease diagnosis pilot returned results to the Genomic Medicine Centers of the English National Health Service from May 2016 through April 2019. It applied Exomiser's phenotype-based prioritization to genomes from 2,183 families. The pilot report appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine on 11 November 2021. Genetic diagnoses were found in 25% of probands, rising to 35% for monogenic disorders. The virtual panel-based pipeline alone made 322 (66%) of the 490 diagnoses that were based on single-nucleotide variants or indels. With Exomiser's ranking, diagnoses were detected in 77% of the top-ranked candidate variants, in 86% of the top three candidates, and in 88% of the top five candidates. Of the 490 diagnoses, 92% came from applied gene panels or Exomiser's top five candidates. Clinicians reported that 134 of 533 genetic diagnoses, 25%, were of immediate clinical actionability, including medication changes, surveillance recommendations, clinical trial eligibility and reproductive planning. The authors report that a diagnosis of CTPS1 deficiency in a 10-year-old girl, admitted to intensive care with life-threatening chicken pox after a seven-year diagnostic odyssey, enabled a curative bone marrow transplantation. They report that a diagnosis of transcobalamin II deficiency, made after a male neonate died at four months with no diagnosis, let his younger brother start weekly hydroxocobalamin injections that prevent metabolic decompensation. The authors do not say whether Exomiser or the applied panels found either variant. In December 2024 Exomiser's developers and a Genomics England scientist reported that a fresh run across the full project found diagnoses for 463 of 24,015 unsolved patients. In January 2025 the Hong Kong Genome Project reported that Exomiser accounted for 107 of 132 diagnoses from single-nucleotide variants and indels in 520 families and ranked 67% of them first. In October 2025 an independent group at the University of Utah and Stanford reported an optimized variant prioritization process for Exomiser and Genomiser, drawn from 386 diagnosed probands of the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. With that process, the percentage of coding diagnostic variants ranked within the top 10 candidates increased from 49.7% to 85.5%.

purpose: Exomiser scores and ranks candidate causative variants against a patient's phenotype, so that clinical teams can manage the diagnosis of rare disease from whole genomes.

ratings.reason: The authors report named proband outcomes. A diagnosis of CTPS1 deficiency in a 10-year-old girl, admitted to intensive care with life-threatening chicken pox after a seven-year diagnostic odyssey, enabled a curative bone marrow transplantation. A diagnosis of transcobalamin II deficiency, made after a male neonate died at four months with no diagnosis, let his younger brother start weekly hydroxocobalamin injections that prevent metabolic decompensation. The authors do not say whether Exomiser or the applied panels found either variant, so the depth rests on the pilot's reported outcomes without an attribution to the software.

The virtual panel pipeline alone made 322 of the 490 diagnoses that came from single-nucleotide variants or indels, and the panels together with Exomiser's top five candidates made 92% of them. That is a measurable gain in what the diagnostic pipeline could find.
A 25% diagnostic yield across 2,183 families is reported for a national pilot. No change across the population is documented.
